stages.title: Advanced grammar
stages.hook: "The teacher praised me" and "I was praised by the teacher". Japanese changes the verb to flip the viewpoint.
explain: The passive (受身, ukemi) is made with -(r)areru: 褒める → 褒められる. 先生に褒められました (I was praised by the teacher). The agent is marked with に. Japanese also has the "suffering passive", used when something unpleasant affects you: 雨に降られました (I got rained on).

The causative (使役, shieki) is made with -(s)aseru: 母は弟を買い物に行かせました (Mother made/let younger brother go shopping). The potential (可能形, kanōkei) says can: 日本語が話せます (I can speak Japanese), where the object often takes が.

Other advanced patterns express judgement. 〜そうだ is "looks like" (from appearance) or "I heard" (hearsay), 〜ようだ is "seems" from evidence, 〜らしい is "apparently", and 〜はずだ is "should be". The conditional ば (if) and なら (if it is the case) differ in nuance.
stages.mnemonic: られる for passive, させる for causative.
sentences: I was praised by the teacher.
Mother made younger brother go shopping.

gq.q: What does 弟を行かせました express?
o: My brother was sent to me
Made or let my brother go
gq.why: The causative expresses making or letting someone do something.

panel.q: What is a "suffering passive"?
o: A passive showing a bad effect on someone
panel.why: It is a passive that shows an unpleasant effect on the speaker.

panel.q: Which pattern shows hearsay?
panel.why: 〜そうだ can mean "I heard that".

panel.q: Why does 日本語が話せます use が?
panel.why: With potential verbs, the object is often marked with が.

teach.model: The passive is -areru, the causative is -saseru and the potential means can. Patterns such as sō da, yō da and rashii express judgement or hearsay.

points.ask: How do I make the passive?

trip.prompt: Find the passive section and read an example of the suffering passive.

stages.title: Complex sentence patterns
stages.hook: "The more you practise, the better you get." Japanese has a neat pattern for that.
explain: Pattern 〜ば〜ほど (ba… hodo) means the more… the more…: 練習すればするほど上手になります (the more you practise, the better you become). 〜にもかかわらず (ni mo kakawarazu) means in spite of: 雨にもかかわらず試合は行われました (despite the rain, the match took place).

〜わけではない (wake de wa nai) means it does not mean that…: 嫌いなわけではありません (it is not that I dislike it). 〜ことにする shows your own decision and 〜ことになる shows a decision made by circumstances: 来年日本へ留学するつもりです (I intend to study in Japan next year).
Other patterns: 〜べき (should), 〜ように (so that, in order to) and 〜はずだ (expected). Choosing between つもり (intention), ことにする (decide) and ことになる (it was decided) is a typical test of usage.
stages.mnemonic: Decide yourself: ことにする. Decided for you: ことになる.
sentences: The more you practise, the better you get.
Despite the rain, the match was held.
I intend to study in Japan next year.

gq.why: 〜ことにする shows your own decision.

gq.q: What does 〜にもかかわらず express?
gq.why: It means despite or in spite of.

panel.q: A manager says 来月から東京で働くことになりました. What does this suggest?
o: It was decided that I will work in Tokyo
panel.why: ことになる shows a decision made by circumstances or others.

panel.q: What does 嫌いなわけではありません mean?
o: It is not that I dislike it
panel.why: It means "It is not that I dislike it".

panel.q: Which pattern fits "the more you read, the more you understand"?
o: 読めば読むほど分かる
panel.why: 〜ば〜ほど matches the more… the more….

teach.model: Patterns such as ~ba ~hodo, ~ni mo kakawarazu and ~wake de wa nai express nuance. ~koto ni suru is your decision, and ~koto ni naru is a decision by circumstances.

points.ask: What is the difference between ~koto ni suru and ~koto ni naru?

trip.prompt: Find the list of N3 or N2 grammar patterns and write two example sentences.

stages.title: Extended conversations
stages.hook: In a real conversation you do not just speak. You nod, you hedge and you shift the topic. Which small words help?
explain: Fillers and responses keep the flow. そうですね (sō desu ne) means "that's right" or "let me see". なるほど (naruhodo) means "I see". たしかに (tashika ni) means "indeed" and やっぱり (yappari) means "as expected". 実は (jitsu wa) introduces a surprising truth: 実は少し迷っています (to tell the truth, I'm a little unsure).

To give opinions softly, use 〜と思います (I think) or 〜かもしれません (maybe). ところで (tokorode) changes the topic ("by the way") and つまり (tsumari) summarises ("in other words"). 例えば (tatoeba) introduces an example.

Japanese speakers often avoid saying no directly. Phrases like ちょっと難しいですね (that's a little difficult) can mean a refusal. Listen for tone, pauses and hedges, and answer with a reason rather than a bare no.
stages.mnemonic: Listen, nod, hedge, then give your reason.
sentences: To tell the truth, I am a little unsure.
I see, that way of thinking is possible too.
By the way, what are your plans tomorrow?

gq.why: ところで changes the topic.

panel.q: A colleague says ちょっと難しいですね about your request. How should you read this?
panel.why: It is often a polite way to refuse.

panel.q: Why is 〜と思います useful in discussions?
panel.why: It softens an opinion.

panel.q: What does つまり do?
panel.why: つまり summarises: in other words.

teach.model: Use そうですね and なるほど to respond, 〜と思います to soften an opinion, and ところで to change the topic. A phrase like ちょっと難しいです can be a polite refusal.

points.ask: How do I soften an opinion?
What does ちょっと難しい suggest?

trip.prompt: Read a dialogue and mark each aizuchi.

stages.title: Formal and informal registers
stages.hook: Speaking to a customer, to a boss and to a friend: the same verb changes shape. This is keigo.
explain: Japanese has plain style (だ), polite style (です・ます, 丁寧語, teineigo) and honorific language (敬語, keigo). Keigo has two main kinds: 尊敬語 (sonkeigo, honorific), which raises the other person's actions, and 謙譲語 (kenjōgo, humble), which lowers your own actions.

Examples: "go/come/be" is いらっしゃる (honorific) and 参る (humble); "eat" is 召し上がる (honorific) and いただく (humble); "say" is おっしゃる (honorific) and 申す (humble). 先生は明日いらっしゃいます (the teacher will come tomorrow); 私が資料をお送りします (I will send the materials).

Never use sonkeigo for your own actions or kenjōgo for the other person's. To a customer, a company employee refers to their own boss in humble terms. Choosing the register depends on the relationship, age, situation, and in-group or out-group status.
stages.mnemonic: Raise them with sonkeigo, lower yourself with kenjōgo.

gq.why: 召し上がる raises the other person's action.
いただく lowers the speaker's own action.

panel.q: A student says 私が先生におっしゃいました. What is wrong?
o: They used humble wrongly for the teacher
panel.why: おっしゃる is honorific and cannot be used for your own action.

panel.q: To a customer, how does an employee refer to the company president?
o: Without raising him too highly, in humble terms
panel.why: Toward outsiders, you lower your own in-group.

panel.q: Which factors affect register choice?
o: Relationship, age, situation and in-group status
panel.why: Relationship, age, situation and in-group status all matter.

teach.model: Keigo has honorific forms to raise another person and humble forms to lower yourself. Use the right kind for the right person, and never use honorific for your own actions.

points.ask: Can I use honorific for myself?

trip.prompt: Make a table of five verbs with plain, honorific and humble forms.

stages.title: Reading articles and literature
stages.hook: "I am a cat. I do not yet have a name." Which famous Japanese novel begins like this?
explain: Reading Japanese texts means meeting different genres: 新聞 (shinbun, newspaper) with its 見出し (midashi, headline) and 社説 (shasetsu, editorial), 小説 (shōsetsu, novel), and poetry. Newspapers use kanji heavily, compact sentences and the plain style.
Natsume Sōseki (夏目漱石) wrote 『吾輩は猫である』 (1905). Its opening lines are 「吾輩は猫である。名前はまだ無い。」 ("I am a cat. As yet I have no name."). The old-fashioned 吾輩 (wagahai) is a proud way to say "I".

A haiku (俳句) has 5-7-5 sounds and usually contains a season word (季語, kigo). Matsuo Bashō (松尾芭蕉) wrote 古池や蛙飛び込む水の音: "An old pond; a frog jumps in, the sound of water." The cutting word や (ya) divides the poem. Reading tips: look for the season, the cut and the images.
stages.mnemonic: 5-7-5 and a season word make a haiku.
sentences: As yet I have no name.
An old pond; a frog jumps in, the sound of water.

gq.q: What is the pattern of a haiku?

panel.q: What is a 季語?
panel.why: A kigo is a word that points to a season.

panel.q: What does the cutting word や do in Bashō's poem?
panel.why: It divides the poem into two images.

panel.q: Why read the headline of a newspaper first?
panel.why: It gives the topic in compact form.

teach.model: Newspapers use headlines and compact sentences. Natsume Sōseki wrote a novel narrated by a cat. A haiku has 5-7-5 sounds and a season word, and often a cutting word.

points.ask: How do I read a newspaper?
Who wrote the novel narrated by a cat?

trip.prompt: Read the opening of I Am a Cat and note the narrator's attitude.

stages.title: Essay and correspondence writing
stages.hook: How do you open and close a formal Japanese letter or email? There are set phrases that tell the reader you are polite.
explain: A formal letter opens with 拝啓 (haikei, "respectfully") and closes with 敬具 (keigu, "yours sincerely"). A seasonal greeting (時候の挨拶, jikō no aisatsu) follows the opening, for example about the weather or the season. Modern emails are shorter.

A business email has a clear subject (件名, kenmei), the recipient's name and company, a greeting such as お世話になっております (thank you for your continued support), the body, and a closing like どうぞよろしくお願いいたします. 添付 (tenpu) means attachment. A signature (署名, shomei) comes last.

Use keigo throughout: 資料を添付いたします (I attach the document). Avoid casual shortenings, and use 様 (sama) for formal addresses, such as 田中様. Check the name, title and kanji, since mistakes in a name are especially rude.
items: thank you for your continued support
お世話になっております
sentences: Thank you for your continued support.
I look forward to your kind cooperation.

gq.q: Which pair opens and closes a formal letter?
gq.why: 拝啓 opens and 敬具 closes.

panel.q: Why is 様 used in 田中様?
o: It is a more formal title than さん
panel.why: 様 is a more formal title than さん.

panel.q: What is wrong with a business email that starts with the recipient's first name only?
panel.why: Business emails use the surname, company and honorific.

panel.q: Why check the kanji of a name carefully?
panel.why: A mistake in someone's name is considered rude.

teach.model: A formal letter opens with 拝啓, a seasonal greeting, the body, and closes with 敬具. Business emails use a subject line, お世話になっております, keigo and 様.

points.ask: How does a formal letter start and end?
What do I write at the start of a business email?
How do I address the recipient?

trip.prompt: Read about business emails in Japan and note one rule.

stages.title: Translation fundamentals
stages.hook: Japanese often leaves out "I" and "you". How should a translator handle that in English?
explain: Translation (翻訳, hon'yaku) means conveying meaning. 直訳 (chokuyaku) is literal translation and 意訳 (iyaku) is free translation. Japanese often omits the subject (主語, shugo): 食べました can mean I ate, you ate or she ate. A translator into English must decide the subject from context (文脈, bunmyaku).

Word order differs. Japanese puts the verb last and modifiers before nouns, so a long sentence is often reordered in English. Politeness level is another challenge: English has no direct equivalent of keigo, so the translator expresses it through word choice or tone.

Idioms need care. 猿も木から落ちる (saru mo ki kara ochiru) literally says "even monkeys fall from trees", meaning anyone can make a mistake. A translator should convey the meaning, not just the monkeys. Mistranslation (誤訳, goyaku) can cause confusion in contracts or manuals.
stages.mnemonic: Find the hidden subject, then reorder.
sentences: A literal translation can be unnatural.
I translate while thinking about the context.

gq.q: What does 猿も木から落ちる mean?
gq.why: It means even experts make mistakes.

gq.q: Why is 食べました hard to translate without context?
gq.why: The subject is omitted, so context decides who ate.

panel.q: What is the best approach to a Japanese idiom?
panel.why: Convey the meaning or an equivalent idiom.

panel.q: Why must a translator reorder a long Japanese sentence?
panel.why: Japanese puts the verb last, while English does not.

panel.q: How can English show Japanese politeness levels?
panel.why: English can use word choice and tone.

teach.model: Japanese omits subjects, puts verbs last and uses keigo. A translator reads the context, chooses the subject, reorders the sentence and translates idioms by meaning.

points.ask: What problem is the omitted subject?

trip.prompt: Compare a literal and a free translation of a Japanese proverb.

stages.title: Regional varieties and cultural context
stages.hook: Does everyone in Japan speak the same? A person from Osaka may say "ookini" for thank you.
explain: The standard Japanese (標準語, hyōjungo, or 共通語, kyōtsūgo) is based on Tokyo speech and is used in education and the media. Dialects (方言, hōgen) vary widely. 関西弁 (Kansai-ben), spoken around Osaka and Kyoto, has features such as おおきに (thank you) and ほんま (really).

Beyond Japanese dialects, the Ryukyuan languages (琉球諸語) of Okinawa and nearby islands are related to Japanese but are usually considered separate languages and are endangered. Ainu (アイヌ語), the language of the Indigenous Ainu people of Hokkaido, is unrelated to Japanese and also endangered.

Regional speech reflects local history and culture. Many Japanese people use standard Japanese at work and dialect at home or with friends, so they switch codes. Dialect words are valued as local heritage, and dialect-based revitalisation projects exist.
stages.mnemonic: Standard for the nation, dialects for the home.
sentences: People in Osaka speak Kansai dialect.
The Ainu language differs from Japanese in origin.

gq.q: What is the standard Japanese based on?
gq.why: Standard Japanese is based on Tokyo speech.

gq.q: Which language is unrelated to Japanese?
gq.why: Ainu is not known to be related to Japanese.

panel.q: Why are Ryukyuan languages usually considered separate languages?
o: They are the same as Kansai-ben
They are written only in English
panel.why: They differ greatly from Japanese and are not mutually intelligible.

panel.q: What does code-switching mean for a Japanese speaker?
o: Using different varieties in different settings
panel.why: Using standard Japanese in some settings and a dialect in others.

panel.q: Why are dialect revitalisation projects important?
panel.why: Dialects and local languages carry heritage and are disappearing.

teach.model: Standard Japanese is based on Tokyo speech. Dialects such as Kansai-ben vary. Ryukyuan languages are related to Japanese but different, and Ainu is unrelated. People switch codes between settings.

points.ask: What is standard Japanese based on?

trip.prompt: Find a map of Japanese dialect regions and note two features.

stages.title: Structured debates and presentations
stages.hook: Give a clear 2-minute talk: how do you open, give reasons and close in Japanese?
explain: A Japanese presentation (発表, happyō) is clear and polite. Open with これから発表を始めます (I will now begin my presentation) and introduce your topic. State your opinion with 私は…と考えます and give reasons with 理由は三つあります (there are three reasons).

In discussions, you can agree (賛成, sansei) or disagree (反対, hantai) politely: 私はこの意見に賛成です. When disagreeing, soften the tone: 少し違う考えを持っています (I have a slightly different view). Support your point with evidence (根拠, konkyo) and examples.

End with a summary (まとめ, matome) and thank the audience: ご清聴ありがとうございました (thank you for your kind attention). Speak slowly, look at the audience and keep your slides simple. Avoid attacking people, focus on ideas.
items: ご清聴ありがとうございました
sentences: Thank you for your kind attention.

o: ご清聴ありがとうございました
gq.why: ご清聴ありがとうございました thanks the audience.
根拠 means grounds or evidence.

panel.q: How can you disagree politely?
o: 少し違う考えを持っています
panel.why: Soften the tone with a mild phrase.

panel.q: What is the purpose of まとめ?
panel.why: It summarises the main points.

panel.q: Why avoid attacking people in debate?
panel.why: Focus on ideas, not on the person.

teach.model: Open with これから発表を始めます, state your opinion, give reasons and evidence, summarise and thank the audience. Disagree politely and focus on ideas.

points.ask: How do I support my view?

trip.prompt: Watch a short Japanese presentation and note its structure.
